problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ have the inner product of Example 1, and let $$\textbf{x} = \left( 1 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ and $$\textbf{y} = \left( 5 \text{,} - 1 \right)$$ .

list.item: Describe all vectors $$\left( z_{1} \text{,} z_{2} \right)$$ that are orthogonal to $$\textbf{y}$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$\mathbb{R}^{2}$$ have the inner product of Example 1. Show that the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality holds for $$\textbf{x} = \left( 3 \text{,} - 2 \right)$$ and $$\textbf{y} = \left( - 2 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ . [Suggestion: Study $$|\left\langle \textbf{x} \text{,} \textbf{y} \right\rangle|^{2}$$ .]

Let $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ have the inner product given by evaluation at $$- 3$$ , $$- 1$$ , $$1$$ , and $$3$$ . Let $$p_{0}(t) = 1$$ , $$p_{1}(t) = t,$$ and $$p_{2}(t) = t^{2}$$ .

list.item: Compute the orthogonal projection of $$p_{2}$$ onto the subspace spanned by $$p_{0}$$ and $$p_{1}$$ .

Find a polynomial $$q$$ that is orthogonal to $$p_{0}$$ and $$p_{1}$$ , such that $$\left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} q \right\}$$ is an orthogonal basis for $$\text{Span} \left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} p_{2} \right\}$$ . Scale the polynomial $$q$$ so that its vector of values at $$\left( - 3 \text{,} - 1 \text{,} 1 \text{,} 3 \right)$$ is $$\left( 1 \text{,} - 1 \text{,} - 1 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ .

problem.paragraph: Let $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ have the inner product as in Exercise 9, with $$p_{0} \text{,} p_{1}$$ , and $$q$$ the polynomials described there. Find the best approximation to $$p(t) = t^{3}$$ by polynomials in $$\text{Span} \left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} q \right\}$$ .

Let $$p_{0}$$ , $$p_{1}$$ , and $$p_{2}$$ be the orthogonal polynomials described in Example 5, where the inner product on $$\text{ℙ} _{4}$$ is given by evaluation at $$- 2$$ , $$- 1$$ , $$0$$ , $$1$$ , and $$2$$ . Find the orthogonal projection of $$t^{3}$$ onto $$\text{Span} \left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} p_{2} \right\}$$ .

Find a polynomial $$p_{3}$$ such that $$\left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} p_{2} \text{,} p_{3} \right\}$$ (see Exercise 11) is an orthogonal basis for the subspace $$\text{ℙ} _{3}$$ of $$\text{ℙ} _{4}$$ . Scale the polynomial $$p_{3}$$ so that its vector of values is $$\left( - 1 \text{,} 2 \text{,} 0 \text{,} - 2 \text{,} 1 \right)$$ .

Let $$A$$ be any invertible $$n \times n$$ matrix. Show that for $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ , the formula $$\text{⟨} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{⟩} = (A\mathbf{u}) \cdot (A\mathbf{v}) = {(A\mathbf{u})}^{T}(A\mathbf{v})$$ defines an inner product on $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ .

Let $$T$$ be a one-to-one linear transformation from a vector space $$V$$ into $$\mathbb{R}^{n}$$ . Show that for $$\mathbf{u}$$ , $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$V$$ , the formula $$\text{⟨} \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \text{⟩} = T(\mathbf{u}) \cdot T(\mathbf{v})$$ defines an inner product on $$V$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: Use the inner product axioms and other results of this section to verify the statements in Exercises 15–18.

problem.paragraph: $$\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} c\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = c\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle$$ for all scalars $$c$$ .
If $$\left\{ \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\}$$ is an orthonormal set in $$V$$ , then $$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} = \sqrt{2}$$ .
$$\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle = \frac{1}{4} \text{∥} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} - \frac{1}{4} \text{∥} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ .
$$\text{∥} \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} + \text{∥} \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2} = 2 \text{∥} \mathbf{u} \text{∥} ^{2} + 2 \text{∥} \mathbf{v} \text{∥} ^{2}$$ .

exercise_group.instruction: In Exercises 19–24, $$\mathbf{u}$$ ﻿, $$\mathbf{v}$$ , and $$\textbf{w}$$ are vectors. Mark each statement True or False (T/F). Justify each answer.

problem.paragraph: (T/F) If $$\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{u} \right\rangle = 0$$ , then $$\mathbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ .
(T/F) If $$\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle = 0$$ , then either $$\mathbf{u} = \textbf{0}$$ or $$\mathbf{v} = \textbf{0}$$ .

(T/F) $$\left\langle \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{v} \text{,} \textbf{w} \right\rangle = \left\langle \textbf{w} \text{,} \mathbf{u} \right\rangle + \left\langle \textbf{w} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle$$ .
(T/F) $$\left\langle c\mathbf{u} \text{,} c\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = c\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle$$ .
(T/F) $$|\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{u} \right\rangle| = \left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{u} \right\rangle$$ .
(T/F) $$|\left\langle \mathbf{u} \text{,} \mathbf{v} \right\rangle| \leq \parallel \mathbf{u} \parallel \parallel \mathbf{v} \parallel$$ .

Given $$a \geq 0$$ and $$b \geq 0$$ , let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} \sqrt{a} \\ \sqrt{b} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} \sqrt{b} \\ \sqrt{a} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to compare the geometric mean $$\sqrt{ab}$$ with the arithmetic mean $$(a + b)/2$$ .

Let $$\mathbf{u} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} a \\ b \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} 1 \\ 1 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ . Use the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to show that $$\left(\left(\right. \frac{a + b}{2} \left.\right)\right)^{2} \leq \frac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2}$$

[T] Let $$\text{ℙ} _{4}$$ have the inner product as in Example 5, and let $$p_{0}$$ , $$p_{1}$$ , $$p_{2}$$ be the orthogonal polynomials from that example. Using your matrix program, apply the Gram–Schmidt process to the set $$\left\{ p_{0} \text{,} p_{1} \text{,} p_{2} \text{,} t^{3} \text{,} t^{4} \right\}$$ to create an orthogonal basis for $$\text{ℙ} _{4}$$ .

[T] Let $$V$$ be the space $$C\lbrack 0 \text{,} 2\pi\rbrack$$ with the inner product of Example 7. Use the Gram–Schmidt process to create an orthogonal basis for the subspace spanned by $$\left\{ 1 \text{,} \text{cos} t \text{,} \cos^{2}t \text{,} \cos^{3}t \right\}$$ . Use a matrix program or computational program to compute the appropriate definite integrals.

By Axiom $$1$$ , $$\left\langle \mathbf{v},\textbf{0} \right\rangle = \left\langle \textbf{0},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$$ . Then $$\left\langle \textbf{0},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = \left\langle 0\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = 0\left\langle \mathbf{v},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle$$ , by Axiom $$3$$ , so $$\left\langle \textbf{0},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle = 0$$ .

By Axioms $$1$$ , $$2$$ , and then $$1$$ again, $$\left\langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} + \textbf{w} \right\rangle = \left\langle \mathbf{v} + \textbf{w},\mathbf{u} \right\rangle = \left\langle \mathbf{v},\mathbf{u} \right\rangle + \left\langle \textbf{w},\mathbf{u} \right\rangle = \left\langle \mathbf{u},\mathbf{v} \right\rangle + \left\langle \mathbf{u},\textbf{w} \right\rangle$$ .
